analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to offer basic health coverage and creates state backstop plans for people private insurers reject.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees and then to three subcommittees, never received a vote, and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This Republican health bill would have amended the nation's employee-benefits law to push every employer to offer a basic health plan or a payroll-deduction plan to its workers, with state-run nonprofit systems as a backstop for people insurers reject because of preexisting conditions. To make coverage cheaper, it would have wiped out state laws that require specific health benefits and state rules that restrict managed care, given new tax breaks to self-employed people, and loosened tax rules for multiple-employer insurance arrangements. It also set up federal grants to states, a study of using practice guidelines to cut malpractice costs, and an advisory council. It never got a hearing vote or a floor vote and expired with the Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured workers and their families would gain a guaranteed offer of at least basic coverage from their employer. People rejected as 'uninsurable' or restricted for preexisting conditions would get coverage through new state systems. Self-employed individuals would see the share of their health insurance they can deduct from taxes rise from 25% to 100% by 1996.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured workers and people with preexisting conditions

how_it_helps.text: Requires each employer to maintain a basic group health plan or a group health payroll deduction plan covering every eligible employee and dependent, with exclusions only for employers in business under two years, those with two or fewer employees, and certain temporary workers.

Directs states to be able to establish nonprofit health benefits systems that must cover people rejected as uninsurable risks and cover material preexisting conditions, with federal grants of $200 million per year for fiscal 1992 through 1994 to help states and approved alternative systems set up universal coverage.
Raises the self-employed health insurance deduction from 25% to 50% in 1994-1995 and to 100% starting in 1996, ending a tax rule that treated the self-employed worse than corporate employees.

Removes IRS restrictions on the tax-exempt status of multiple employer welfare arrangements (MEWAs) that provide basic health benefits, letting small employers band together to buy coverage, subject to new annual reporting to state insurance commissioners.

analysis.who_pays: Patients would give up state-mandated benefit requirements and state protections around managed care, since the bill preempts both for employer plans. The federal Treasury would fund the grants and lose revenue from the larger self-employed deduction. Employers above the smallest size would bear compliance costs, though the payroll-deduction option requires no employer contribution.
analysis.who_pays_short: State insurance rules, taxpayers, and mid-size employers

drawbacks.text: The employer requirement is weak: an employer can comply simply by offering a payroll-deduction plan that withholds the worker's own wages, with no employer contribution required, so a worker who cannot afford the premium gets the form of coverage but not the money to buy it.

The bill preempts state laws that require specific health benefits or provider coverage in employer plans and preempts state restrictions on managed care, stripping away state consumer protections in order to let insurers sell stripped-down, lower-cost plans.

The basic benefit package is only a floor whose depth is left to future HHS regulations, and state system coverage is made secondary to employer plan coverage, limiting how much these systems actually help people who also have an employer plan.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's goal — universal access to at least basic coverage — is real, and the state backstop for uninsurable people and preexisting conditions was ahead of its time. But the design leans heavily on the insurance market: the employer 'requirement' lets employers shift the whole premium onto workers, the affordability gains come partly from erasing state-mandated benefits and managed-care protections, and the self-employed tax break is a straight revenue loss weighted toward higher earners. It is a genuine expansion framework with real consumer-protection trade-offs, and it was poorly matched to the Democratic House, which never acted on it.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in three House committees and then three subcommittees after its March 1991 referral, and no committee or floor vote ever happened before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Fred Grandy (R-IA) and six original Republican cosponsors introduced the bill on March 5, 1991; four more Republicans added their names in September 1991, for 10 Republican cosponsors in total.

The bill was referred jointly to the Committees on Education and Labor, Energy and Commerce, and Ways and Means on the day of introduction, then routed to the relevant health and labor subcommittees in mid-March 1991.
No markup, hearing vote, or floor action followed; the last recorded action is the March 21, 1991 subcommittee referral, and the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained from the bill's death: the uninsured got nothing, though state governments and insurance regulators kept their existing authority over mandated benefits and managed care, and employers avoided the new coverage requirement.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; state regulators kept authority

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; the Democratic-controlled House committees took no action on the bill after referral.

industries.note: The bill routes universal coverage through employer-based private plans and state nonprofit systems, guaranteeing insurers a customer base, and loosens tax rules for multiple-employer arrangements. But it also preempts state benefit mandates, letting insurers sell stripped-down plans, so patient protections would shrink even as the industry's role is locked in.

The bill preempts state laws restricting managed care, including rules on provider networks, rate-setting, and utilization review, opening states up to managed-care expansion. That could lower premiums through competition but removes state consumer protections over how plans restrict care.

The deduction for self-employed health insurance rises from 25% to 100% by 1996, a direct tax benefit. The cost is forgone federal revenue, and the benefit is worth most to those with the highest incomes.

Employers with more than two employees and two years in business must maintain a coverage option, but the payroll-deduction alternative requires no employer contribution, so the compliance cost is modest while workers bear the premium. Smallest and newest employers are exempt.

States gain a federally supported framework and grants to build nonprofit health benefits systems covering uninsurable people. At the same time, federal preemption takes away their power to require specific benefits or regulate managed care in employer plans.
